events.title: Three Times Three #5
events.fullDescription:
The room is small enough that you can hear the dancers' feet on the floor before the music starts. Three musicians sit on one side. Three dancers stand on the other. Nobody knows who will work with whom until the moment arrives — the pairings are drawn at random, and each duo gets fifteen minutes to build something from nothing. You are watching the negotiation happen in real time.

Three Times Three is a monthly improvisation series curated by composer Spyros Polychronopoulos (known as Spyweirdos) at the Κέντρο Ελέγχου Τηλεοράσεων — the Television Control Center — in Athens. The format is precise: three musicians meet three dancers, random pairs improvise for fifteen minutes each, and then all six performers join for a thirty-minute collective improvisation to close the evening. Edition number five brings together drummer Yiannis Notaras, saxophonist Dimitris Pantelias, and vocalist Anastasia Kotsali alongside dancers Maria Kasidokosta, Dorothea Polychronopoulou, and Anastasia Valsamaki. The performers come from contemporary dance and experimental music backgrounds, and the improvisation operates at a professional level — this is not a jam session.

The crowd for a series like this draws from two communities that rarely overlap elsewhere: the contemporary dance circuit and the experimental music scene. You will find choreographers watching how musicians respond to physical cues, and sound artists studying how dancers translate rhythm into gesture. The audience is small by design — this is not programming that aims to fill a stadium, and the intimacy is the point.

| Aspect | Details |
|--------|---------|
| **Setting** | Television Control Center, Kyprou 91A — compact performance space, industrial character |
| **Vibe** | Experimental, curious, collaborative — the audience is part of the negotiation |
| **Sound** | Drums, saxophone, voice — acoustic, unmediated, reacting in real time |
| **Door** | Ticketed, walk-in welcome |

The evening builds through accumulation. The first duo finds its language — maybe the drummer follows the dancer's breath, maybe the dancer resists the rhythm entirely. The second pairing discovers a different dynamic. By the third, the audience has learned to read the improvisation alongside the performers. The closing collective piece draws on everything that came before, and the six performers must navigate each other's vocabularies simultaneously. Some editions produce moments of startling precision; others reveal productive friction. Neither outcome is a failure.

If you want a polished performance with a known setlist and rehearsed transitions, improvisation series operate on different terms — the risk of the unknown is the offer. But if you are drawn to the moment where a saxophonist and a dancer find a shared pulse without speaking a word, and you want to witness that discovery happening fifteen minutes at a time, Three Times Three makes the process visible.

The Television Control Center is at Kyprou 91A and Sikinou 35, in the Ampelokipoi area. Start time is 21:00. Tickets are €10 — available through more.com or by calling 213 00 40 496. The venue is not directly on a metro line, but Ampelokipoi metro on the Blue line is a fifteen-minute walk, and taxis from the center run €8-10. The monthly cadence means missing one edition is not permanent — but each edition's random pairings produce combinations that will not recur.

No two editions of Three Times Three produce the same performance, because the format guarantees that the performers cannot prepare for each other. This is the fifth iteration, which means the series has earned its audience — and the format has proven resilient enough to keep generating surprises.

events.title: Joanna Mattrey
events.fullDescription:
You push through the door into a basement that smells of vinyl and wood. Record crates line the walls on your left; to your right, a small performance space where the acoustic treatment turns every scrape of a bow into something deliberate. Eighty people at capacity. Tonight there are maybe fifty chairs set out, and the performer is close enough that you can see rosin dust lift off the strings.

Joanna Mattrey is a New York-based violist, composer, and improviser whose work sits at the boundary between contemporary classical and free improvisation. She studied at the New England Conservatory and has performed alongside Tyshawn Sorey, Henry Threadgill, Marc Ribot, John Zorn, and Elliott Sharp — musicians who treat improvisation as architecture, not decoration. Her solo albums "Veiled" and "Dirge," both released on independent labels, explore the viola through extended techniques, electronic alterations, and compositions that function as frameworks for real-time decision-making. She is also a certified Alexander Technique teacher, which shapes how she approaches the physical act of playing — the instrument becomes an extension of breath and posture, not just fingers and bow.

Underflow draws a crowd that knows what it is coming to hear. Experimental music listeners who track releases on Relative Pitch Records. Sound artists who treat a Friday basement show as seriously as a gallery opening. Musicians from the Athens improvisation scene who come to study technique at close range. Conversation happens before and after, not during.

| Aspect | Details |
|--------|---------|
| **Setting** | Basement venue beneath a record store, ~80 capacity, acoustically treated |
| **Vibe** | Focused, quiet, specialist — a room for concentrated listening |
| **Sound** | Acoustic-forward, intimate enough to hear the instrument's full range of texture |
| **Door** | Ticketed, walk-in friendly for early arrivals |

A Mattrey performance does not follow the arc of verse-chorus-verse. Expect extended passages where the viola produces sounds you did not know the instrument contained — harmonics that shimmer, percussive bowing that cracks like static, sustained drones that settle into the room like weather. The compositions leave space for improvisation, and the improvisations carry compositional weight. Pieces unfold rather than progress.

If you want melody-driven music or a social evening with conversation and drinks, Underflow on a night like this asks for something different — stillness, attention, and patience with sounds that build on their own time. But if you are the kind of listener who finds a single sustained note more interesting than a chord progression, and you want to hear an improviser who has shared stages with John Zorn and Henry Threadgill working in a room this small, this is why you came to Koukaki tonight.

Underflow is in the Koukaki neighborhood, a short walk from Syngrou-Fix metro station on the Red line. Doors at 21:00. Tickets are €10 — for a performer who sells out ISSUE Project Room in New York, this is Athens pricing at its most generous. The venue doubles as a record store, so arrive early to browse. Cash and cards accepted. The room fills from the front, and the front rows offer a proximity to the instrument that changes what you hear.

An international improviser of Mattrey's caliber playing a room this small only happens because Athens' experimental scene operates at a scale where intimacy is still possible. Underflow programs roughly one show like this per week. They are rarely repeated.

events.title: Ο βυσσινόκηπος
events.fullDescription:
The curtain hasn't gone up yet and you can already feel the weight of the room. The Central Stage of the National Theatre's Tsiller Building holds its history in the walls — Chekhov was last performed here forty-one years ago, and the air feels like it remembers. You settle into your seat and the house lights drop to the sound of eleven voices finding their registers, as if tuning instruments before the first note.

Hector Lygizos directs The Cherry Orchard — Chekhov's final play — treating the text as a musical score and the actors' voices as the instruments that carry it. His adaptation, in Chrysa Prokopaki's translation, follows a Russian family unable to save the orchard that defines them, watching their world dissolve while they argue about whether to act. It is Chekhov's most unsparing comedy: everyone on stage knows what must be done, and nobody does it. The National Theatre last staged this work on its Central Stage in 1984, directed by Giorgos Michailidis, and before that in 1966 under Takis Mouzenidis. Lygizos' production is only the third in sixty years to occupy this specific room.

The ensemble of eleven includes Amalia Moutsou, Rania Oikonomidou, Yvonne Maltezou, and Giorgos Ziakas — actors whose stage experience carries the "musical realism" Lygizos pursues. This is a production built on collective precision rather than star turns.

| Aspect | Details |
|--------|---------|
| **Setting** | Central Stage, Tsiller Building — the National Theatre's main room, formal proscenium |
| **Vibe** | Weighted, attentive, institutional — the flagship stage for a reason |
| **Sound** | Voice-driven, text-as-music approach — clarity over spectacle |
| **Door** | Ticketed, assigned seating |

The production finds its rhythm in what Lygizos calls Chekhov's "cheerful yet heartbreaking tragicomedy." Scenes of aristocratic paralysis play against moments of genuine tenderness. The orchard is not just real estate — it is a way of life ending while its owners argue over tea. You will recognize the impulse to postpone what cannot be postponed.

If you want fast-paced modern staging with projections and electronic scores, this production stays closer to Chekhov's own tempo — deliberate, character-driven, built on silences. But if you want to hear Chekhov's final work performed as its author intended — slowly, with every pause earning its weight — in a room that has hosted Greek theater since the building opened, this is the production.

The Tsiller Building sits at Agiou Konstantinou 22-24, walkable from Omonoia metro on either the Red or Blue line. Performances run Wednesday and Sunday at 17:00, Thursday through Saturday at 20:00. Tickets range from €5 for special categories to €25, available through ticketservices.gr. The run extends through early April, but opening weeks draw the most invested audiences. Accessibility performances with Greek Sign Language interpretation and audio description are scheduled for March 12 and 13.

Three productions of The Cherry Orchard on this stage in sixty years. The interval between the second and third was four decades. You will not wait another four decades to form an opinion — but the next chance to see Chekhov here may be further off than you think.

events.title: Ο ΑΓΑΠΗΤΙΚΟΣ ΤΗΣ ΒΟΣΚΟΠΟΥΛΑΣ (ΓΙΑ ΠΕΡΙΟΡΙΣΜΕΝΟ ΑΡΙΘΜΟ ΠΑΡΑΣΤΑΣΕΩΝ)
Το μαγικό εισιτήριο
events.fullDescription:
The lights are soft and the floor is covered in cushions. You settle down with your child in your lap, eye-level with the performer, and the room hums with the small sounds of toddlers discovering that the space belongs to them. A dancer moves slowly across the stage with a veil that catches the light, and forty pairs of small eyes follow it like a flock tracking a bird.

Το μαγικό εισιτήριο is a forty-minute performance created by Sara Toscano — dancer, creator, and narrator — together with musician Solis Barkis, under the direction of Lambros Fisfis. It is designed for babies from ten months to three years old, accompanied by a parent or caregiver. The production uses movement, original music by João Farinha, and simple props — balls, veils, balloons — to build a sensory world where a ball becomes a planet and a veil becomes a wave through the logic of play. Toscano trained in dance and physical theater, and her movement vocabulary here is calibrated for an audience that does not yet distinguish between performer and playmate.

The crowd is exactly who you would expect: parents and grandparents with toddlers in various states of wonder, crawling, and occasional protest. The room is designed for unpredictability — no one expects silence, and the performers treat every small interruption as part of the show. You will find other parents who are relieved to be in a space where a child's noise is welcomed rather than tolerated.

| Aspect | Details |
|--------|---------|
| **Setting** | Giannis Marinos Hall at Megaron — intimate hall, audience on floor cushions |
| **Vibe** | Gentle, exploratory, joyful — a performance that meets children on their terms |
| **Sound** | Live music, soft and responsive to the room's energy |
| **Door** | Ticketed, open seating on cushions — arrive early for spots near the front |

The show follows the journey of a girl with a magic ticket, but the narrative is secondary to the experience. What holds a toddler's attention is not plot but texture — the way a balloon floats, how fabric moves through air, the moment when a musical phrase makes a child rock forward on the cushion. Toscano and Barkis read the room in real time, adjusting pace and proximity to match the collective energy of the youngest audience members.

If your child is older than three, they will likely find the pacing slow and the content simple. If your child startles at sudden sounds or movement, the production is gentle enough that this is rarely an issue — but every child is different, and the performers expect a range of responses. If you are looking for structured children's theater with a clear story, this is more sensory exploration than narrative.

Megaron is directly adjacent to Megaro Moussikis metro station on the Blue line. The Giannis Marinos Hall is on the lower level — follow signs from the main entrance. Performance time is 10:30 on Sundays, with select weekday dates during school holidays. Tickets are €20 for one child and one adult, €28 for two children and one adult. Purchase online through the Megaron website or at the box office. Plan to arrive fifteen minutes early — cushion seating is first-come, first-served. Stroller parking is available in the lobby.

The Magic Ticket has been running since November 2025, which means the production team has had months to refine what works for this audience. Performances designed for children under three are rare in Athens — Megaron is one of the few institutions that programs them, and this run continues through late March 2026.

Μήδεια Έξοδος ΙΙΙ
events.fullDescription:
The marble figures watch from their pedestals as you enter a room that was built to hold sculpture, not audiences. Footsteps echo off stone floors. The air carries the cool, mineral stillness of a gallery after hours, and somewhere behind you, a counter-tenor's voice begins to fill the space with a sound that has no clear origin.

Μήδεια Έξοδος ΙΙΙ is a site-specific theater work staged inside the National Glyptotheque in Goudi, among the permanent collection of Greek sculptor Yianoulis Halepas. Director Konstantinos Chatzis — founder of the Chroma theater company, trained in the physical theater traditions of Lecoq and Brook — has built a dramaturgical synthesis that places Euripides' Medea text in direct conversation with Halepas' sculptures. The music of Giorgos Koumendakis anchors the production: his 1991 composition "Eros Demon," written for counter-tenor and two pianos on the poetry of Sappho, becomes the emotional spine of the performance. Koumendakis composed the music for the 2004 Athens Olympic ceremonies; here his work operates at chamber scale, winding through gallery rooms rather than filling a stadium.

The audience for this kind of work self-selects. You will find theater regulars who track Chatzis' projects across unconventional spaces, contemporary music listeners who know Koumendakis from the concert hall, and gallery visitors who discovered the production through the National Gallery's own programming. The common thread is curiosity about what happens when disciplines collide in a space designed for none of them.

| Aspect | Details |
|--------|---------|
| **Setting** | National Glyptotheque sculpture halls, Goudi — former royal stables converted to gallery |
| **Vibe** | Concentrated, immersive, site-specific — art within art |
| **Sound** | Counter-tenor and two pianos, live, resonating off stone walls |
| **Door** | Ticketed entry, limited capacity per performance |

The production moves through the gallery rooms as a living installation. Euripides' text follows the arc of a refugee woman — Medea as exile — while the Halepas sculptures around you become silent witnesses to her displacement. The counter-tenor's voice fills corridors designed for contemplation, not performance. Each room shifts the acoustic, so the experience changes as you move with the production through the space.

If you prefer traditional proscenium theater with clear sightlines and comfortable seating, this is not that. But if you are drawn to the intersection of ancient text, contemporary music, and physical space — where the venue itself becomes a character — this production uses the Glyptotheque in a way that cannot be replicated elsewhere.

The venue is at Alsos Stratou (Army Park) in Goudi, with the entrance off Katechaki Avenue. Katechaki metro station on the Blue line puts you within a ten-minute walk. Performances run Wednesday through Sunday from February 25 to March 15. Arrive early to orient yourself in the gallery — the sculptures you see before the performance begins are the same ones that frame the action. The space is not heated to gallery standards, so bring a layer in February.

No other theater production in Athens this season puts Euripides inside a sculpture museum with a Koumendakis score performed live among the works of Halepas. The combination exists here, for three weeks, and then it does not.

events.title: Louis C.K. - Ridiculous
events.description: με τον Louis C.K.. O βραβευμένος με Emmy Αμερικανός Louis C.K., γνωστός για το ωμό και αμφιλεγόμενο στυλ του επί σκηνής παρουσιάζει τη νέα του παράσταση, κατάλληλη...
events.fullDescription:
The house lights dim and the Christmas Theater contracts around a single figure at center stage. Louis C.K. with a microphone and whatever accumulated observations he's decided to share tonight. No props. No projected visuals. No comfort blanket of production values. Just language delivered with precision.

"Ridiculous" marks Louis C.K.'s second Athens date, continuing a European tour that's proven demand persists despite — or perhaps because of — everything that changed his career's trajectory. The comedy hasn't softened. If anything, the years since his public reckoning have sharpened the writing, adding layers of self-examination to material that was already unflinching. He's not asking for forgiveness; he's analyzing the condition.

The crowd that fills the Christmas Theater for night two has made a specific choice. They've processed the debates about separation between art and artist and decided to be present. The laughter arrives in complex waves — sometimes pure amusement, sometimes uncomfortable recognition, sometimes the particular sound of an audience not sure if they're allowed to find something funny. Louis has been working this tension for years now.

The Christmas Theater handles this show with technical competence — strong sightlines, acoustics calibrated for spoken word, seating that keeps even the distant rows connected to the stage. But the real work happens in the space between comedian and audience, that fragile transaction of trust and discomfort that defines live stand-up.

If you want comedy that provides escape, that leaves you lighter than you arrived, Louis C.K. in 2026 isn't designed for that. He's processing darkness publicly, finding humor in places most people don't want to look. But if you believe the best comedy emerges from genuine risk, from a performer willing to alienate portions of his audience in pursuit of something true — you understand why this room is full.

events.fullDescription:
You settle into a candlelit table as the first notes of a Brazilian guitar fill the room. The warmth of bossa nova wraps around you while the scent of wine mingles with the low hum of conversation. This is where Athens comes to remember that music can be both sophisticated and sensual.

Miranda Verouli leads her quintet through a tribute to Gal Costa, the Brazilian singer whose voice defined tropicália and MPB for five decades. Costa's catalog—from the psychedelic experimentation of the late 1960s to the romantic ballads that made her a household name—gets reimagined for an intimate jazz club setting.

The crowd here knows their music. You'll find vinyl collectors who can debate the relative merits of Costa's Tropicália albums, couples who slow-danced to these songs in their youth, and younger listeners discovering this repertoire for the first time. Nobody's checking their phone.

| Aspect | Details |
|--------|---------|
| **Setting** | Intimate jazz club, ~150 capacity, low ceilings amplify every note |
| **Vibe** | Warm, romantic, conversational |
| **Sound** | Listening room—every brush on the snare audible |
| **Seating** | Tables with full service, bar stools for solo visitors |

The set builds from quiet acoustic arrangements through to the full-blooded samba that Costa made her own. Expect the quintet to find new angles on familiar melodies.

If you want loud or want to dance—this isn't it. But if you're the kind of person who listens to albums start to finish and appreciates musicians who've studied their craft for decades, pull up a chair.

events.title: «Nina Simone - 4 οκτάβες Ελευθερίας»
events.fullDescription:
The Arroyo Theater darkens and something in the air shifts. You're about to spend an evening with Nina Simone — not the woman herself, but the music, the legacy, the four octaves that contained multitudes. A tribute performance faces impossible standards. This one leans into that impossibility.

"4 Octaves of Freedom" — the title captures what made Simone singular. That voice spanned everything from whispered intimacy to full-throated righteous fury, often within the same song. She was classically trained yet bluesy, technically precise yet emotionally unguarded. The tribute performer taking this on understands they're not imitating — they're channeling.

The audience for Nina Simone tribute shows brings particular expectations. You'll find people who know every album, who can tell you which version of which song they prefer. There are those discovering her through this entry point, led here by covers they've heard or recommendations they've received. And there are those for whom Simone represented something political, who heard freedom in those four octaves before anyone called it protest music.

The Arroyo Theater provides an appropriate setting — intimate enough that the emotional weight of this material lands, but substantial enough to contain the moments when the music opens up. Simone's catalog includes quiet devastation and soaring triumph, and both need room to breathe.

If you want a nostalgic greatest-hits cabaret, a comfortable trip through familiar melodies, this production likely has other ambitions. Simone's music was never comfortable. She made songs that forced audiences to feel things they'd rather avoid. A tribute that honors her would do the same. But if you're ready to experience what those four octaves carried — freedom, yes, but also pain, rage, beauty, and defiance — you're in for an evening that earns its title.

| **Doors** | 20:00 |
| **Show** | 21:00 |
| **Venue** | Arroyo Theater, Athens |

Four octaves carried everything Nina Simone needed to say. The tribute attempts the same.

Η Αθήνα από την Ανατολή στη Δύση 1821-1896
events.description: Η Αθήνα από την Ανατολή στη Δύση 1821-1896 Πώς ήταν η Αθήνα, μια μικρή οθωμανική πόλη, στις αρχές του 20ού αιώνα; Πώς σε λιγότερο από έναν αιώνα μεταμορφώθηκε σε μια νεοκλασική πόλη που φιλοξένησε με
events.fullDescription:
The Megaron's main hall fills with an audience carrying specific historical awareness. Tonight's program traces Athens through 75 years — 1821 to 1896, from revolutionary capital of a newborn nation to established European city. The music is the vehicle; the history is the destination.

"Athens 1821-1896" represents programmatic ambition. The selection spans the music that accompanied the city's transformation — from the folk melodies of a recently liberated people through the classical compositions that marked Greece's entry into European cultural life. Each piece carries context: this is what Athens sounded like during the reign of Otto, during the Megali Idea period, during the first modern Olympics.

The audience for historically-themed concerts brings particular engagement. These are listeners who understand the dates referenced, who can place musical choices in political and social context. You'll find history enthusiasts alongside music devotees, each finding different entry points into the same material. The program notes become companions to the performance.

The Megaron Mousikis provides the ceremonial weight this kind of historical project requires. The main hall's capacity and acoustic excellence match the ambition of the programming. When the orchestra plays music from a specific era, the setting amplifies the sense of occasion — this is Athens now, honoring Athens then.

If you want pure musical entertainment divorced from historical narrative, this program's scholarly framework might feel constraining. The evening works best for those who want both — beautiful music and the story it tells. But if you're curious about how Athens sounded to itself during its first 75 years as a modern capital, if you want to experience musical nation-building — this is the concert that attempts that synthesis.

This exhibition represents the current state of dialogue between artificial intelligence and visual art. The pieces on display emerged from processes that involve machine learning, generative systems, and artistic curation working in concert. The question hanging over every work: what happens when creativity becomes computational? The answers here are multiple and contradictory.

The audience for this kind of exhibition brings tech-curious alongside art-curious. You'll find people approaching from software backgrounds, trying to understand the artistic choices. You'll find traditional art viewers confronting unfamiliar production methods. The conversations that happen in gallery corners touch on authorship, intentionality, beauty, and what any of those words mean when algorithms get involved.

The Megaron's exhibition spaces provide the institutional weight this material needs. These questions aren't fringe anymore — they're being asked in major cultural venues, given the presentation context that signals seriousness. The curation treats the works as art first, technology second, even while the technology is the subject.

If you need traditional hand-made objects and human authorship clearly established, this exhibition will unsettle you. That's partly the point — to examine assumptions about where art comes from and what counts. But if you're ready to engage with questions that will only become more pressing as these technologies develop, if you want to see how artists and institutions are beginning to frame the algorithmic — this is how Athens joins that conversation.

The lights come up on a stage that's been set for revelation. You're in one of those theaters where the architecture demands attention, but tonight the focus pulls toward a single figure. Nikolas Smyrnakis prepares to disappear into characters who share more than a name.

"Likes Attract" works on a premise that sounds simple until you watch it unfold. Smyrnakis plays homonymous characters — people who share names but nothing else. Or so it seems. As the evening progresses, the connections between these separate lives start surfacing in ways that feel earned rather than forced. The comedy comes from recognition, the drama from what we recognize in ourselves.

Smyrnakis has built a reputation in Greek theater for performances that layer humor over something more unsettling. His timing operates at the edge between laugh and wince. Tonight's material gives him room to shift between personas, each distinct enough to feel like different actors, similar enough to create the evening's central tension. The writing matches the performer — smart without announcing itself.

The crowd filtering into these multiple venues carries the particular energy of Greek theater audiences. These are people who follow performers across productions, who remember Smyrnakis from earlier work and came specifically for what he brings. Conversations before curtain compare notes on previous shows, establishing the shared context that makes insider references land. By intermission, strangers are debating which character works best.

Greek comedy theater operates differently than its English-language counterpart. The rhythms are faster, the physical comedy broader, the emotional pivots sharper. If you're not fluent in Greek, you'll catch the physicality but miss the wordplay. Smyrnakis builds much of his comedy on language — puns, double meanings, the music of Greek syllables doing their work.

The venues hosting "Likes Attract" have been selected to match the production's scale. Intimate enough that Smyrnakis can play the back row without amplification, large enough to generate the collective energy that comedy requires. When the room laughs together, it laughs as a single organism.

If you need your theater in English or prefer spectacle over substance, this night will frustrate you. The humor operates in Greek at native speed, no subtitles, no concessions. The material Greka performs tonight spans that era — not just the famous songs but the deeper catalog that reveals the full range of what Vembo meant.

Parnassos provides the acoustic and atmospheric context this material requires. The hall has hosted similar evenings for generations — the kind of performance where Greek cultural memory gets transmitted to new ears. The audience tonight spans ages, some who remember Vembo's voice from childhood radios, others discovering the songs through this contemporary lens.

The crowd at Parnassos concerts carries the particular reverence of people for whom this music is heritage. These aren't casual attendees but pilgrims of a sort. Conversations before curtain compare memories, debate which songs should have made the setlist. The silence when Greka begins is absolute — the kind of attention that performance at this level earns.

If you need English lyrics or contemporary reference points, this evening will leave you at a distance. Vembo's significance requires Greek context, historical awareness, the ability to hear how these songs functioned when they first aired. But if you've been looking for entry into Greek musical heritage, for a performer who can bridge decades without betraying either side — Parnassos holds this evening for you.

events.title: ΠΑΣΧΑΛΗΣ ΤΟΝΙΟΣ «ΑΞΙΟΣ ΛΟΓΟΣ»  ΚΩΣΤΗΣ ΠΑΛΑΜΑΣ - 83 χρόνια μετά
ΜΕΣΑ ΣΤΟ ΜΥΑΛΟ ΣΟΥ- Dr. Γιώργος Λάγιος- Part 2
Πόσα τσιγάρα έχω καπνίσει από τότε που έφυγες
Πώς μιλάει η μουσική για τον εαυτό της;
BLUES CARGO Special Guest Michael Dotson
events.fullDescription:
The harmonica wails and the room transforms. Cigarette smoke may be banned these days, but close your eyes and you could be in a Delta juke joint circa 1955. Blues Cargo have been keeping this flame alive in Athens for decades, and tonight they've brought reinforcements.

Michael Dotson joins Blues Cargo as special guest, bringing American blues authenticity to a band that's spent years perfecting the form. This is blues played by musicians who've studied the original recordings until they could hear the room, not just the notes.

Blues audiences in Athens are a dedicated tribe. You'll find them in faded band t-shirts from shows they actually attended, discussing the finer points of different Chicago blues eras between sets. These are people who own more vinyl than their shelves can hold.

| Aspect | Details |
|--------|---------|
| **Setting** | Intimate club, exposed brick and low lighting |
| **Vibe** | Loose, warm, knowing |
| **Sound** | Amplified but never harsh—you'll feel the bass in your chest |
| **Seating** | Tables clustered around the stage, bar at the back |

The night builds from slow blues to shuffles to the kind of extended jams that only happen when musicians trust each other completely. With a special guest, expect some improvised moments that won't be repeated.

If you need polish and production, if blues feels like history homework—this won't convert you. But if a bent note can raise the hair on your arms, don't miss this.

| Info | Details |
|------|---------|
| **Date** | Monday, March 2, 2026 |
| **Doors** | 21:00 |
| **Music starts** | 21:30 |
| **Duration** | ~2.5 hours |
| **Price** | €15-20 table / €10-15 bar |
| **Tickets** | halfnote.gr |
| **Address** | Trivonianou 17, Mets |
| **Getting there** | Akropoli Metro (Red Line), 10 min walk |
| **Last metro** | 00:15 (show ends in time) |
| **Payment** | Cards and cash |
| **Good to know** | Monday shows are easier to book—but still reserve |

Half Note on a blues night offers something Athens' slick modern venues can't: the feeling of music made in the moment, for the people in the room.

**Tags:** Jazz, Intimate, Local-favorite, Mixed-ages, Metro-accessible, Reservation-required

**Last verified:** February 2026
